sections.name: Logical Reasoning
sections.description: Two scored sections on the LSAT (~24–26 questions each, 35 minutes per section). Each question presents a short argument or set of facts followed by a single multiple-choice prompt. LR tests the ability to analyze, evaluate, and complete arguments — the core daily work of a lawyer.
sections.format: ~25 standalone short-passage questions; 5 answer choices labeled A–E.
sections.scoring: Roughly 50% of the scaled score weight (two LR sections out of four scored sections).
skills: Spot reasoning flaws (causal, conditional, sampling, equivocation, …)
tips: Always identify the conclusion before evaluating the answers.
On flaw questions, name the flaw in your own words first.
Pre-phrase the right answer for assumption / strengthen / weaken before reading the choices.

sections.name: Reading Comprehension
sections.description: One scored section: four passages (one is typically a comparative pair) drawn from law, humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, followed by 5–8 questions each. Tests close reading, structural mapping, and the ability to distinguish what the author claims from what the author merely reports.
sections.format: ~27 questions across 4 passage sets; 5 answer choices A–E.
sections.timing: 35 minutes total (~8:30 per passage including reading time).
sections.scoring: Roughly 25% of the scaled score weight.
skills: Identify main point, author attitude, and tone
Compare two passages on the comparative-reading set
tips: Read for STRUCTURE first, details second — questions reward knowing where to look.
Annotate authorship moves: claims, contrasts, examples, hedges.
Pre-phrase the main point before reading the answer choices.
Eliminate extremes for tone questions unless the passage is explicit.

sections.name: Analytical Reasoning (Logic Games)
sections.description: Historically four games per scored section (sequencing, grouping, matching, hybrid). LSAC announced a multi-year phase-out of the dedicated LG section beginning in August 2024 — replaced by an additional Logical Reasoning section on the August 2024 LSAT and beyond. Logic Games remain pedagogically essential: the diagramming skills they develop transfer directly to LR conditional reasoning and to legal exam writing. Practice them.
sections.format: Each game presents a setup + ~3–6 rules followed by 5–7 questions sharing the same setup; 5 answer choices A–E.
sections.scoring: Phasing out for the operational LSAT in 2024–2025; still scored on older PrepTests and many practice batteries.
tips: Spend the first 60–90 seconds turning the rules into a clean visual diagram.
On orientation questions, eliminate one answer per rule.
On 'if'-then questions, build the hypothetical and force every implication before reading the answers.
If you find more than two solutions for a 'must be true' question, you're missing an inference.

concepts.name: Alternative Cause
concepts.summary: A confounding variable that explains the observed pattern equally well or better.
concepts.detail: Most LR weaken answers introduce an alternative cause. Strengthen answers usually rule one out.

concepts.name: Appeal to Ignorance
concepts.summary: Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence (or vice versa).
concepts.detail: 'No one has shown X is true, therefore X is false' — and its mirror 'No one has shown X is false, therefore X is true.' Both are flawed because lack of evidence settles nothing.

concepts.name: Author's Attitude / Tone
concepts.summary: Identify the author's stance toward the subject — endorsement, skepticism, neutrality, etc.
concepts.detail: Look for evaluative adjectives, hedge words ('arguably', 'risks'), and rhetorical questions. Hedged language usually means a hedged answer (qualified concern, cautious optimism) is right.

concepts.name: Causation vs. Correlation
concepts.summary: Inferring cause from a mere correlation is a classic LR flaw.
concepts.detail: When an argument says 'X and Y are correlated, therefore X causes Y', look for: (a) reverse causation (Y → X), (b) common cause (Z → both), (c) coincidence, (d) selection bias. Weaken answers usually surface one of these alternatives.
examples: Breakfast eaters score higher on cognitive tests → eating breakfast causes cognitive performance? Could be sleep, exercise, or socioeconomic confounders.

concepts.name: Conditional Reasoning
concepts.summary: Working with 'if/then' statements, their contrapositives, and chains of conditionals.
concepts.detail: Indicators: 'if', 'only if', 'unless', 'whenever', 'all', 'every', 'no', 'none'. 'Only if' attaches to the *necessary* condition; 'unless' translates to '¬X → Y'. Always diagram conditionals before answering and always check the contrapositive.
examples: Only members may vote → Vote → Member (and ¬Member → ¬Vote).
Unless you submit by Friday, your filing is late → ¬Submit-by-Friday → Late.

concepts.name: Contrapositive
concepts.summary: The contrapositive of 'P → Q' is '¬Q → ¬P'; logically equivalent.
concepts.detail: Contraposition is the workhorse of LR conditional questions. Note: the *converse* (Q → P) and the *inverse* (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT equivalent — confusing them is the affirming-the-consequent / denying-the-antecedent flaw.
examples: P → Q is equivalent to ¬Q → ¬P, but not to Q → P or ¬P → ¬Q.

concepts.name: Could Be True EXCEPT
concepts.summary: Four answers are possible in some valid layout; one is impossible. Pick the impossible.
concepts.detail: Treat as a 'must be false' question. Construct counter-examples for the four 'could' options; the remaining choice is your answer.

concepts.name: Detail Question
concepts.summary: Ask what the passage explicitly states. Always go back to the text.
concepts.detail: The right answer is paraphrased directly from a specific sentence; trap answers are inferences (correct, but not stated) or close-but-not-quite restatements.

concepts.name: Rule-Elimination
concepts.summary: Quickly knock out 'could be the order' answer choices by checking one rule at a time.
concepts.detail: On orientation questions, scan the answers rule-by-rule rather than building a master diagram. Each rule typically eliminates exactly one answer.

concepts.name: Equivocation
concepts.summary: Using one word in two different senses across an argument.
concepts.detail: Tricky because the equivocated term is often subtle ('volume of submissions' vs. 'diversity of viewpoints', or 'theory' as 'guess' vs. 'theory' as 'scientific framework'). Watch for shifts in scope between the premise and conclusion.

concepts.name: Flaw in the Reasoning
concepts.summary: Identify the logical error the argument commits.
concepts.detail: Common flaws: ad hominem, circular reasoning, equivocation, hasty generalization, sampling bias, appeal to ignorance, false dichotomy, conflating correlation with causation, part-whole conflations, conditional reasoning errors (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent).

concepts.name: Grouping Game
concepts.summary: Select or distribute entities into groups under membership rules.
concepts.detail: Two families: selection (in/out of one group, e.g. 'choose four of seven') and distribution (partition into teams). Diagram membership conditionals ('If J is in, K is out' → J → ¬K) and chain contrapositives. Numeric limits (group sizes) drive most hard inferences.
examples: If J is selected then K is not; if K is not selected then L is. Selecting J forces L.

concepts.name: Main Conclusion
concepts.summary: Identify the statement the rest of the argument exists to support.
concepts.detail: The main conclusion is what everything else supports and what supports nothing further. Indicator words help ('therefore', 'thus') but the LSAT loves burying the conclusion first or mid-argument and decorating premises with conclusion-like language. Test a candidate by asking 'does anything in the argument support THIS?' — if yes, keep climbing.
examples: 'Since the statute is ambiguous, and ambiguous statutes are construed against the drafter, the clause should be read narrowly.' Main conclusion: read the clause narrowly.

concepts.name: Main Point Question
concepts.summary: Identify the central thesis of the passage.
concepts.detail: The main point summarizes the WHOLE passage, not a single paragraph. Wrong answers are usually too narrow (a single example) or too broad (a vague abstraction).

concepts.name: Method of Reasoning
concepts.summary: Describe HOW the argument proceeds, not whether it succeeds.
concepts.detail: Common techniques: counterexample, analogy, reductio ad absurdum, eliminating alternatives, appealing to a general principle, attacking a premise vs. attacking reasoning. The credited answer describes the move at the right abstraction level; traps describe techniques the argument never uses or misidentify the target of an objection.
examples: 'Opponents claim X; but X implies Y, and Y is absurd; so not-X' — a reductio.

concepts.name: Modus Ponens
concepts.summary: Valid conditional inference: if P then Q; P; therefore Q.
concepts.detail: The simplest valid conditional inference. Distinguish from the *invalid* mirror moves — affirming the consequent (Q ∴ P) and denying the antecedent (¬P ∴ ¬Q) — both classic LR flaw types.
examples: All senior partners have argued before the supreme court. Maria is a senior partner. ∴ Maria has argued before the supreme court.

concepts.name: Modus Tollens
concepts.summary: Valid conditional inference: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
concepts.detail: Modus tollens is the contrapositive form. Whenever a conditional 'P → Q' is true, the contrapositive '¬Q → ¬P' is logically equivalent. The LSAT loves to test contrapositive recognition because students who only memorize 'P → Q' miss that the same rule also tells you what happens when Q fails.
examples: If the contract is enforceable, both parties signed. The contract was not signed by both parties. ∴ The contract is not enforceable.

concepts.name: Must Be True
concepts.summary: An answer that holds in every case consistent with the given statements.
concepts.detail: In LG: build the hypothetical, force every implication, then evaluate each answer — if even one valid layout makes the answer false, it doesn't 'must be true'. In LR: the credited inference must follow strictly from the stimulus; watch for quantifier downgrades ('all' → 'most' → 'some') and reversed conditionals in the traps.

concepts.name: Necessary Assumption
concepts.summary: An unstated premise the argument REQUIRES in order to hold.
concepts.detail: Use the negation test: negate the candidate; if the argument collapses, it was necessary. Necessary assumptions are minimally helpful — they fill the smallest possible gap, not the most ambitious.
examples: Argument: 'A or B; not A; ∴ B.' Necessary assumption: those were the only options.

concepts.name: Parallel Reasoning
concepts.summary: Match the abstract STRUCTURE of the stimulus, not its subject matter.
concepts.detail: Diagram the stimulus as variables (P, Q, R…). Then test each answer choice by diagramming it the same way. The correct answer must match the validity status (valid ↔ valid, invalid ↔ same kind of invalid) and the structural shape.

concepts.name: Principle Application
concepts.summary: Match a general rule to the concrete case that satisfies all of its conditions.
concepts.detail: Treat the principle as a conditional with (possibly several) trigger conditions and an exception clause. The conforming case satisfies every trigger and no exception. Traps satisfy most-but-not-all conditions, trip the exception, or run the principle backwards (concluding the trigger from the result).
examples: Principle: a lawyer may withdraw only if withdrawal will not prejudice the client. Case that conforms must show BOTH withdrawal AND no prejudice.

concepts.name: RC Inference
concepts.summary: What the passage most strongly supports beyond its explicit statements.
concepts.detail: Unlike detail questions, the credited answer is not stated — it follows from combining two or three passage claims. It stays modest: hedged language in the passage yields hedged inferences. Traps are real-world plausible but textually unsupported, or turn 'some commentators argue' into the author's own view.
examples: Passage: defenders cite discovery abuse; critics cite access. Supported inference: the parties disagree about which cost matters more — NOT that either side would abolish pleading standards.

concepts.name: Passage Structure
concepts.summary: Map each paragraph's role: setup, complication, evidence, counter-argument, resolution.
concepts.detail: Before answering questions, jot a one-line label for each paragraph. Most RC question types (main point, author attitude, role of statement, function of paragraph) become trivial once the structural map is clear.

concepts.name: Tone
concepts.summary: Closely related to author attitude — measure intensity (mild/strong) and polarity (positive/negative).
concepts.detail: Eliminate extremes ('uncritical', 'open hostility') unless the passage explicitly supports them.

concepts.name: Resolve the Paradox
concepts.summary: Find the fact that lets two apparently conflicting findings both be true.
concepts.detail: The stimulus reports a surprising discrepancy ('sales rose while ad spending fell'). The credited answer adds information that dissolves the tension without denying either finding. Wrong answers explain only one side, deepen the mystery, or drift out of scope.
examples: Fewer traffic tickets were issued, yet accident rates fell. Resolver: cameras replaced officers and deter violations without issuing tickets.

concepts.name: Sequencing Game
concepts.summary: Place items in a strict order (1st through nth) under constraints.
concepts.detail: Diagram with slots. Render rules as adjacency blocks (F-H), distance constraints, and forbidden positions. Make a hypothetical for any rule that creates few options.

concepts.name: Strengthen Question
concepts.summary: Pick the answer that, if true, most supports the argument.
concepts.detail: Mirror image of weaken: rule out alternative explanations, supply a missing assumption, or provide additional confirming evidence.

concepts.name: Sufficient Assumption
concepts.summary: An assumption strong enough to GUARANTEE the conclusion.
concepts.detail: Sufficient-assumption answers can be much stronger than necessary ones. The trick is to map the gap between premise and conclusion and find the answer that closes it completely.

concepts.name: Universal Instantiation
concepts.summary: From 'all P are Q' and 'x is P', conclude 'x is Q'. Always valid.
concepts.detail: The bedrock valid argument form. Distinguish from 'most P are Q' (probabilistic) and 'some P are Q' (existential).

concepts.name: Weaken Question
concepts.summary: Pick the answer that, if true, most undermines the argument.
concepts.detail: Identify the conclusion, then attack the link between premise and conclusion — typically by surfacing a counter-example, alternative cause, or unmet assumption. Avoid answers that simply contradict a premise (the LSAT treats premises as given).

passages.title: Five Associates, One Hearing
passages.summary: Sequencing game: order five associates in five consecutive slots subject to three rules.
passages.setup: Exactly five associates — F, G, H, J, and K — argue exactly one motion each at a single hearing. The motions are heard one at a time, in five consecutive time slots numbered 1 through 5 (1 is first, 5 is last). The order in which they argue is subject to the following constraints:

passages.title: From Code Pleading to Notice Pleading
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph excerpt on the evolution of federal civil procedure pleading standards.
passages.passage:
For most of the nineteenth century, common-law pleading required plaintiffs to fit their grievances into rigid formal categories — assumpsit, trespass on the case, trover. A misstep in selecting the proper writ could doom an otherwise meritorious claim. Reformers complained that the system rewarded procedural sophistication rather than substantive justice; the Field Code of 1848 in New York attempted a partial remedy by replacing the writ system with a unified civil action grounded in 'fact pleading.'

Fact pleading, however, generated its own pathologies. Courts disagreed about how granular the underlying facts had to be, and judges could dismiss a complaint for failing to plead a legally-significant element with sufficient specificity. By the 1930s a generation of procedural scholars — Charles Clark prominent among them — argued that the goal of pleading should be merely to give the defendant fair notice of the claim. The expensive work of testing factual sufficiency belonged in discovery and on summary judgment, not at the courthouse door.

This vision shaped the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which took effect in 1938. Rule 8(a)(2)'s requirement of 'a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief' was a deliberate softening: the 1938 drafters knew they were trading some doctrinal predictability for procedural access. Conley v. Gibson (1957) cemented the bargain when the Supreme Court declared that a complaint should not be dismissed unless it was beyond doubt that no set of facts could support recovery.

The modern picture is more contested. Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007) and Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009) introduced a 'plausibility' threshold that some commentators read as a partial restoration of fact pleading. Defenders of the cases note that mass-tort and antitrust complaints had created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen. Critics counter that the new standard risks reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle, particularly for pro se litigants and civil-rights plaintiffs who often cannot satisfy plausibility without the discovery they are seeking.

passages.title: The Fall of the Privity Requirement
passages.summary: A 4-paragraph excerpt tracing American products-liability law from the privity bar through negligence to strict liability.
passages.passage:
Through most of the nineteenth century, a consumer injured by a defective product could rarely recover from its manufacturer. The doctrine of privity of contract, crystallized in the English case Winterbottom v. Wright (1842), held that a manufacturer's duty ran only to the party with whom it had directly contracted. A coachman maimed when a defective mail coach collapsed could not sue the supplier, because his employer, not he, had purchased the vehicle. Courts defended the rule as a necessary shield for a young industrial economy, reasoning that unlimited liability to remote users would chill manufacturing. The price of that protection fell on injured consumers, who were left without a remedy against the parties best positioned to prevent the harm.

The first decisive crack came in MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. (1916). Writing for the New York Court of Appeals, Judge Benjamin Cardozo held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to any foreseeable user of a product that is reasonably certain to place life and limb in peril when negligently made, regardless of privity. MacPherson did not abolish the need to prove fault; an injured plaintiff still had to show that the manufacturer had been negligent. But by untethering duty from the contract of sale, Cardozo reframed the question as one of foreseeability, and within two decades most American jurisdictions had followed.

Proving negligence, however, remained a formidable obstacle, since the relevant evidence usually lay in the manufacturer's exclusive control. In a celebrated 1944 concurrence in Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co., Justice Roger Traynor urged courts to abandon fault altogether and hold manufacturers strictly liable for injuries caused by defective products. His view prevailed a generation later: Greenman v. Yuba Power Products (1963) imposed liability without proof of negligence, and the Restatement (Second) of Torts §402A (1965) codified strict liability for products sold in a defective condition unreasonably dangerous to the user. A plaintiff now needed to establish only a defect, causation, and injury.

Whether this represented a clean break is debatable. Strict liability was justified largely on the ground that manufacturers could spread the cost of injuries across all consumers through pricing and insurance — a rationale of risk distribution rather than moral fault. Yet in design-defect cases courts increasingly asked whether a product's risks outweighed its utility, an inquiry that looks suspiciously like the reasonableness balancing at the heart of negligence. The modern law of products liability thus sits uneasily between two theories, and its strict-liability label can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it.

questions.stem:
Every senior partner at the firm has argued at least one case before the state supreme court. Maria is a senior partner at the firm. Therefore, Maria has argued at least one case before the state supreme court.

The argument above is most similar in its reasoning to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All birds have feathers. A penguin is a bird. So a penguin has feathers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most lawyers own at least one suit. Therefore, the lawyer next door owns a suit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who passed the bar studied. Tom studied, so Tom passed the bar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If it rains, the picnic is canceled. The picnic was canceled, so it rained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No senator is under 30. Lin is 28, so Lin might be a senator.

questions.explanation: The original is a valid universal-instantiation argument: 'All P are Q; x is P; therefore x is Q.' Choice A has identical form. B uses 'most' (probabilistic). C affirms the consequent. D denies the antecedent reversed. E contradicts a universal.

questions.stem:
City planner: Building a light-rail line will reduce traffic congestion downtown, because every comparable city that built one saw congestion fall within five years.

Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The light-rail line will be more expensive than the planner estimates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some downtown residents oppose the construction noise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light-rail riders in those cities reported high satisfaction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparable cities all simultaneously enacted downtown congestion-pricing tolls.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed line will run mostly underground.

questions.explanation: The argument infers causation from correlation across comparable cities. D introduces a confound — congestion-pricing tolls — that may explain the congestion drop instead of the rail line, undermining the causal inference. A attacks cost (irrelevant to congestion). B, C, and E are off-point.

questions.stem:
If the contract is enforceable, then it was signed by both parties. The contract was not signed by both parties.

Which one of the following can be properly concluded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contract is enforceable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contract is not enforceable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contract is partially enforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only one party intended to be bound.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nothing can be concluded about enforceability.

questions.explanation: Modus tollens: 'If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.' If enforceable required both signatures and we lack both signatures, the contract is not enforceable. The other options either affirm the consequent, add facts not given, or reject a valid inference.

questions.stem:
Editor: Our new policy requires every opinion piece to cite at least three primary sources. Critics claim this will reduce the diversity of viewpoints we publish, since fewer freelance writers have access to primary sources. But our submission rate has not dropped since the policy took effect, so the critics are mistaken.

The editor's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a necessary condition as if it were sufficient.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assumes without warrant that all freelance writers lack primary sources.

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to consider that some published pieces cite more than three sources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a general rule from a single anecdote.

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the volume of submissions with the diversity of viewpoints in those submissions.

questions.explanation: The critics' claim is about *diversity of viewpoints*. The editor rebuts using *submission volume*. Equating the two is the flaw — submission count and viewpoint diversity are different measures, so E names it. A, B, C, and D mischaracterize the structure.

questions.stem:
Studies show that people who eat breakfast perform better on cognitive tests in the morning than people who skip breakfast. Therefore, eating breakfast causes improved cognitive performance.

The argument's reasoning is flawed because it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on studies that may not be representative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to specify what counts as breakfast.

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers causation from correlation without ruling out alternative explanations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that all cognitive tests measure the same ability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: ignores that some people perform well without breakfast.

questions.explanation: Classic correlation ≠ causation flaw. People who eat breakfast may also sleep more, exercise, or have less stress — any of which could be the real cause. The argument fails to rule out these confounders. A, B, D, E are peripheral.

questions.stem:
Columnist: Supporters of the new zoning ordinance say it will preserve the neighborhood's historic character. But the supporters have not produced any architectural surveys to back up that claim. So the ordinance will not preserve the historic character.

The columnist's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: presupposes what it sets out to prove.

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a sample that is too small.

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an individual from claims about a group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats absence of evidence as evidence of absence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: appeals to popular opinion rather than to facts.

questions.explanation: Lack of supporting evidence does not establish the opposite conclusion (the ordinance might still preserve the character even if no survey has been produced). This appeal-to-ignorance flaw is captured by D. A, B, C, and E describe errors the columnist did not commit.

questions.stem:
Lawyer: To win the appeal, the defendant must show either that the trial court misapplied the statute or that the jury was improperly instructed. The trial court did not misapply the statute. So if the defendant wins the appeal, then the jury was improperly instructed.

The lawyer's reasoning depends on which one of the following assumptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are no other grounds on which the appeal could be won.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The defendant will win the appeal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Showing improper jury instructions is sufficient to win an appeal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The jury was in fact improperly instructed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Misapplication of the statute would have been the stronger ground.

questions.explanation: The argument lists two ways to win and rules one out, then concludes the other must be the route to a win. That move only works if those two were the *only* possible grounds. Choice A makes that necessary assumption explicit. B, C, D, and E add facts the argument neither states nor requires.

questions.stem:
Researcher: Patients who received the new therapy recovered faster than those who received the standard treatment. So the new therapy must be more effective than the standard treatment.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The new therapy is more expensive than the standard treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some patients given the standard treatment also recovered quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two groups of patients were similar in age, overall health, and severity of illness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researcher has studied the standard treatment for many years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few patients given the new therapy reported mild side effects.

questions.explanation: Moving from 'recovered faster' to 'more effective' assumes the two groups were comparable to begin with. C rules out the alternative that the new-therapy group was simply healthier, strengthening the causal claim. A and E raise cost and side-effects, which are irrelevant to effectiveness. B and D neither support nor close the gap.

questions.stem:
Only employees who completed the safety course may operate the forklift. No temporary worker has completed the safety course.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some temporary workers may operate the forklift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every employee who completed the safety course operates the forklift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who operates the forklift is a temporary worker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Completing the safety course is sufficient to be allowed to operate the forklift.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No temporary worker may operate the forklift.

questions.explanation: 'Only those who completed the course may operate' means operating requires completion (operate → completed). The contrapositive is ¬completed → ¬operate. Since no temporary worker completed the course, no temporary worker may operate the forklift — E. A contradicts this. B and D treat a necessary condition as if it were sufficient. C reverses the conditional.

questions.stem:
Critic: If a film is a commercial success, it will be widely imitated. This year's top-grossing comedy has already spawned a dozen imitators. So it was a commercial success.

The critic's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it…

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a condition that guarantees an outcome to be required for that outcome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a result that the premise says would follow from success as if it established success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on a sample of films that is too small to support a generalization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that what is true of one comedy is true of all comedies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the popularity of a film with its artistic merit.

questions.explanation: The premise says success → imitation. The critic observes imitation and infers success, affirming the consequent — imitation could arise for other reasons. B names this error. A describes the converse mistake (necessary vs. sufficient) the critic did not make. C, D, and E raise issues the argument does not turn on.

questions.stem:
Anyone who understands the proof will pass the exam. Therefore, Dana will pass the exam.

The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dana understands the proof.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dana has studied harder than anyone else in the class.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Everyone who passes the exam understands the proof.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most students who understand the proof pass the exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anyone who passes the exam will later understand the proof.

questions.explanation: This is a sufficient-assumption question: find the premise that, added to 'understands the proof → passes the exam,' guarantees the conclusion that Dana passes. Only A does it — if Dana understands the proof, the rule forces the conclusion that Dana passes. B is irrelevant (studying is not the stated trigger). D is merely probabilistic ('most'), so it cannot guarantee the result. C and E reverse the conditional (pass → understand), which never licenses concluding that Dana passes.

questions.stem:
If the witness is credible, then the alibi holds. If the alibi holds, then the defendant was not at the scene. The witness is credible.

If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The defendant was not at the scene.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The alibi does not hold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The witness is not credible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the defendant was not at the scene, then the witness is credible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defendant was at the scene.

questions.explanation: Chain the conditionals — credible → alibi holds → not at scene — and apply modus ponens to the given fact that the witness is credible. The conclusion that follows is that the defendant was not at the scene (A). B and C contradict the premises. D reverses a conditional (affirming the consequent) and is not guaranteed. E directly contradicts the valid conclusion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Common-law courts have always preferred bright-line rules to flexible standards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Modern federal procedure has eliminated all procedural barriers facing pro se litigants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drafters of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure rejected the influence of the common-law tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Twombly and Iqbal returned the federal courts to nineteenth-century pleading standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The shift from rigid pleading to notice pleading reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access.

questions.explanation: The passage's central thesis is that the move to notice pleading was a *trade-off*: the drafters knowingly sacrificed some predictability to widen the courthouse door. E captures both halves. A overstates ('always'). B is contradicted by the closing paragraph. C is too strong — the passage says drafters were *informed by* the tradition, not that they rejected it. D confuses the post-Iqbal tightening with a full reversion.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Twombly and Iqbal is best described as one of…

choices.label: A
choices.text: uncritical endorsement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: open hostility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified concern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: scholarly bewilderment.

questions.explanation: The author concedes that the cases addressed real problems (mass-tort fishing expeditions) but worries they 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That hedged worry is qualified concern (C), not endorsement, hostility, indifference, or bewilderment.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure took effect in…
questions.explanation: Detail question. The passage states that 'the original Federal Rules of Civil Procedure … took effect in 1938.' 1957 is the year of Conley v. Gibson; the other dates appear nowhere as the adoption year.

questions.stem: The author mentions the Field Code of 1848 primarily in order to…

choices.label: A
choices.text: argue that fact pleading was superior to the notice pleading that followed it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: show that New York courts led all other jurisdictions in procedural innovation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the writ system was never genuinely abandoned.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that procedural reform inevitably fails.

questions.explanation: The Field Code is introduced as a 'partial remedy' to the writ system, but the next paragraph explains that 'fact pleading … generated its own pathologies.' B captures that role — an early reform that helped yet created new problems. A and E overstate the point; C and D assert claims the passage never makes.

questions.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that defenders of Twombly and Iqbal believe that…

choices.label: A
choices.text: notice pleading should be abolished entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: pro se litigants rarely file meritorious claims.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson was wrongly decided from the outset.

choices.label: D
choices.text: changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Field Code offered a better model than the Federal Rules.

questions.explanation: Defenders 'note that mass-tort and antitrust complaints had created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen' — i.e., new litigation conditions warrant a tougher standard, which is D. A, B, C, and E go well beyond anything the defenders are said to claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Privity of contract was an indefensible doctrine that nineteenth-century courts should have abandoned far sooner than they did.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American products-liability law moved from a privity bar through negligence to strict liability, yet strict liability retains substantial elements of negligence reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick eliminated the requirement that an injured consumer prove a manufacturer's negligence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Torts settled the long-running dispute over the proper basis of manufacturer liability.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola was the most influential single opinion in the history of American tort law.

questions.explanation: The passage traces an arc — privity bar, then negligence after MacPherson, then strict liability — and closes by stressing that strict liability still 'sits uneasily' with negligence reasoning. B captures both the arc and that tension. A states an evaluative claim the author never makes. C is false: the passage says MacPherson 'did not abolish the need to prove fault.' D is contradicted by the final paragraph, which says the question is still 'debatable.' E overstates a detail and is not the passage's overall point.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the doctrine of privity of contract was crystallized in which one of the following cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Winterbottom v. Wright.

choices.label: B
choices.text: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escola v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greenman v. Yuba Power Products.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conley v. Gibson.

questions.explanation: Detail question. The first paragraph states that privity of contract was 'crystallized in the English case Winterbottom v. Wright (1842).' MacPherson (B) cracked the privity rule; Escola (C) and Greenman (D) belong to the strict-liability story; Conley v. Gibson (E) is a civil-procedure case that does not appear in this passage at all.

questions.stem: The author refers to Justice Traynor's concurrence in Escola primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that strict liability had already become the governing rule by 1944.

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify an early judicial argument for strict liability that courts would adopt only later.

choices.label: C
choices.text: criticize the Escola majority for reasoning that was internally inconsistent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that Cardozo's approach in MacPherson had been formally overruled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that risk distribution is an inadequate justification for liability.

questions.explanation: The passage presents the 1944 concurrence as urging a change that 'prevailed a generation later' in Greenman (1963) and §402A (1965) — i.e., an early argument adopted only afterward, which is B. A misreads the timeline (it was a concurrence, not the governing rule). C and D describe moves the author never makes. E states a critique the author raises only as one side of a 'debatable' question, not the reason for citing Traynor.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward describing modern products-liability law as 'strict' is best characterized as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic agreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured skepticism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: outright rejection of strict liability as a concept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference to how the doctrine is labeled.

choices.label: E
choices.text: nostalgia for the privity requirement.

questions.explanation: In the final paragraph the author concedes strict liability's risk-distribution rationale but warns that the 'strict-liability label can obscure how much negligence reasoning survives within it' — a hedged, doubting stance toward the label, i.e., measured skepticism (B). A is too positive. C overstates: the author questions the label, not the doctrine's existence. D is wrong because the author plainly cares about the label's accuracy. E finds no support; the author calls privity a remedyless 'price' borne by consumers.

questions.stem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the associates argue, from first to fifth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: F, G, H, J, K

choices.label: B
choices.text: G, F, H, K, J

choices.label: C
choices.text: K, F, H, J, G

choices.label: D
choices.text: F, H, K, J, G

choices.label: E
choices.text: H, F, G, J, K

questions.explanation: Apply the rules as eliminators. A puts F first and H third — not the required immediate F-H block (Rule 1). B places J fifth, violating Rule 2 (J fourth). C starts with K, violating Rule 3. E reverses the block, putting H before F (Rule 1). D — F, H, K, J, G — satisfies all three: F is immediately before H, J is fourth, and K is not first.

questions.stem: If H argues third, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: F argues first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: K argues second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: J argues fifth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: K argues third.

choices.label: E
choices.text: G argues first.

questions.explanation: If H=3, Rule 1 forces F=2. Rule 2 fixes J=4. Slots 1 and 5 remain for G and K, and Rule 3 forbids K=1, so G=1 and K=5. Therefore E — G argues first — must be true. A is false (F=2); B and D misplace K (K=5); C is false (J=4).

questions.stem: If G argues fifth, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: K argues third.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H argues first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: J argues fifth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: F argues second.

choices.label: E
choices.text: K argues first.

questions.explanation: If G=5, the F-H block (Rule 1) and J=4 (Rule 2) leave only one valid layout: F=1, H=2, K=3, J=4, G=5. So A — K argues third — must be true. E is forbidden by Rule 3; B, C, and D are inconsistent with the forced layout.

questions.stem: Which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: K argues fifth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H argues first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: G argues third.

choices.label: D
choices.text: F argues second.

choices.label: E
choices.text: K argues third.

questions.explanation: Only three orders satisfy the rules: F-H-G-J-K, F-H-K-J-G, and G-F-H-J-K. In every one the F-H block places H in slot 2 or 3, so H can never argue first — B cannot be true. K fifth (A), G third (C), F second (D), and K third (E) each occur in at least one valid order.

questions.stem: If K argues third, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H argues first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: F argues second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: G argues fifth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: G argues first.

choices.label: E
choices.text: H argues fourth.

questions.explanation: If K=3 and J=4 (Rule 2), the F-H block (Rule 1) can only fit in slots 1-2, leaving slot 5 for G. The single valid order is F, H, K, J, G. So C — G argues fifth — must be true. A and D misplace G and H, B places F second (F=1), and E puts H fourth (H=2).
